question: Each of \(2010\) boxes in a line contains a single red marble, and for \(1 \le k \le 2010,\) the box in the \(k\)th position also contains \(k\) white marbles. Isabella begins at the first box and successively draws a single marble at random from each box, in order. She stops when she first draws a red marble. Let \(P(n)\) be the probability that Isabella stops after drawing exactly \(n\) marbles. What is the smallest value of \(n\) for which \(P(n) \lt \dfrac{1}{2010}?\)
solution:
To stop on draw \(n\), Isabella must draw white from the first \(n-1\) boxes and red from box \(n\). Box \(k\) has \(k\) white marbles and one red marble, so its white probability is \(k/(k+1)\), and its red probability is \(1/(k+1)\).

The draws come from separate boxes, so the relevant color events are independent. For \(2\le n\le2010\), multiplying their probabilities gives
\[
P(n)=\left(\frac12\cdot\frac23\cdots\frac{n-1}{n}\right)\frac1{n+1}.
\]
Every numerator from \(2\) through \(n-1\) cancels with the preceding denominator. Only the endpoints remain:
\[
P(n)=\frac1n\cdot\frac1{n+1}
=\frac1{n(n+1)}.
\]
For \(n=1\), the probability is directly \(1/2\), which agrees with the same formula.

All denominators are positive. Thus
\[
P(n)<\frac1{2010}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n(n+1)>2010.
\]
The product \(n(n+1)\) increases as the positive integer \(n\) increases. Since
\[
44\cdot45=1980<2010,
\qquad
45\cdot46=2070>2010,
\]
every \(n\le44\) fails and \(n=45\) succeeds. Therefore the smallest value is \(\boxed{45}\), choice \(\text{A}\).
